issues.passage: Reviewers called her method unrivaled, then named three approaches that surpassed it on every measure.
issues.why: "Called her method unrivaled" is correct, natural use of unrivaled = better than all others. The later contradiction is only pragmatic inconsistency by the reviewers; it does not make the word itself a misuse. A student who knows the definition would accept the wording as valid usage.

fix.correctPassage: The archive remains unrivaled in its coverage of early print culture.
wrongPassages: Scouts called the prospect unrivaled to mean every team had already found a stronger alternative.
The program’s unrivaled outcomes placed it last among district schools in both retention and test gains.
Investors dismissed the design as unrivaled, meaning it offered nothing distinct from existing products.

issues.passage: Historians claimed the treaty prefigured the war only after hostilities had already ended.
issues.why: Natural parse: historians made the claim only after the war ended. "The treaty prefigured the war" is correct use of prefigure = early sign of something later; retrospective claims are normal historical analysis. Not a misuse of the word.

fix.correctPassage: Those early sketches already prefigure the building’s final silhouette.
wrongPassages: Historians said the armistice prefigured the war that had ended the year before.
The sequel is said to prefigure the original novel by repeating plot points readers already know.
Analysts expect the new data to prefigure past recessions by arriving years after those downturns.
